narration: We start with the first input modality: a stack of RGB video frames showing a person moving over time.
Below it comes the second modality, a matching stack of pressure-mat frames that record where the body presses on the floor at each moment.
Each stream is fed to its own encoder. The snowflake on the image encoder marks it as frozen, so only the rest of the network is trained.
An LSAM block then follows each encoder, aggregating the per-frame features along the time axis within its own modality.
Both branches meet in the Fusion Cross-Attention Module, or FCAM, which combines the visual and pressure features into one representation.
The fused features pass to the regressor, the head that turns them into human body parameters.
It predicts theta, the body pose, and T, the global translation of the body in the scene.
From pose and translation the model computes the 3D joint positions, J of theta and T, and then projects them to the image plane with an orthographic projection.
Four losses supervise this chain: pose and translation losses on the parameters, a 3D loss on the joints, and a 2D loss on their projection.
On the right we see what the model produces: a reconstructed motion sequence running from standing, through crouching, to sitting on the ground.
A fifth loss, the contact loss, uses the pressure signal. The inset highlights the contact regions on the soles, keeping the predicted body anchored to the floor.
Now we zoom into the FCAM block. The image feature is projected into a value and a key, while the pressure feature is projected into a query.
Key and query are multiplied and passed through a softmax to form attention weights, which are then multiplied with the image value.
The attended result is added to a residual image-feature skip, refined by a position-wise feed-forward layer, and concatenated with the pressure feature on the way out.
Finally, the legend: the circled cross is a matrix multiplication, the circled plus is an addition, and the circled C is a concatenation.
